ety.text: From Middle English foster, from Old English fōstor (“food, sustenance”), from Proto-West Germanic *fōstr, from Proto-Germanic *fōstrą (“nourishment, food”). Cognate with Middle Dutch voester (“nursemaid”), Middle Low German vôster (“food”), Old Norse fóstr (“nurturing, education, alimony, child support”), Danish foster (“fetus”), Swedish foster (“fetus”).

senses.d: Providing parental care to children not related to oneself.
The care given to another; guardianship.
To nurture or bring up offspring, or to provide similar parental care to an unrelated child.
To promote the development of something; to cultivate and grow a thing.
ex: Our company fosters an appreciation for the arts.

⁠A flower beat with rain and wind,
Which once she foster’d up with care

senses.d: To be nurtured or trained up together.
ex:
There Florimell, in her first ages flowre,
And passing beautie did eftsoones reveale,
Was fostered by those Graces
A griesly Foster forth did rush.
